newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco speeds up financial reforms in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Morocco speeds up financial reforms in 1997.

text.p: Morocco is speeding up monetary and financial reforms in a bold move to open its economy more to the world global market, analysts said.
Morocco will implement soon a law to expand activities of the forex market.

"Local banks will be allowed a currency cross and exchanges of hard currencies with foreign banks," Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj told a meeting of the monetary policy-making National Council of Money and Saving on Tuesday.
A local foreign exchange market was set up last year to stimulate the money market, officials said.

"By enlarging the forex market, Morocco shows it is heading for total liberalisation of the market and convertibility of its currency," Mouna Lahlou, analyst at Casablanca Finance Intermediation said.
Kabbaj told the meeting the Moroccan economy benefited from a record harvest in 1996 which lifted real Gross Domestic Product growth by 11.8 percent after 1995's fall of 6.7 percent.
Morocco's GDP is estimed at 315 billion dirhams ($35 billion) in 1996 against 277 billion ($307 billion) in 1995, an official said.
"The resumption of growth in 1996 was good signal as it took place in a drop of inflation to 3.0 percent from 6.1 percent in 1995, due to the stability of food stuff prices" Kabbaj said.
He said the 1996 growth will have also a multiplying positive impact on other economic sectors this year.
The minister said the current account deficit was reduced to 2.1 percent from 4.7 percent in 1995.

Trade deficit fell to 9.3 percent from 11.9 percent in 1995, bringing the cover ratio to 72.7 percent in 1996 from 68.6 percent in 1995. Tourism receipts and transfers of Moroccan workers abroad rose respectively by 21.1 percent and 6.0 percent.
The minister urged local banks to cut the interest rates on banking loans for small amd medium-sized firms.
He said Morocco plans to set up "a second market" for trading small growing companies to boost economic integration.

"It is a positive initiative which the authorities have taken...There is a real potential for a second market because a great number of Moroccan companies need funds to expand," Hassan Ait Ali, head of Upline Securities stockbroker told Reuters.
The new market will represent launching-pad for the growing firms, to enter the Casablanca bourse in future.

The law sets a minimum of 15 million dirhams ($1.66 million) to introduce a firm on the bourse.Morocco has 6,000 companies with a limited capitalisation level preventing them from entering the stock market.

"I am not sure that the commercial banks would respond immediately to the call of Kabbaj because it will affect their short term profitability...The banks have already reduced their interest rates by 0.25 percent last year," a banker said.
Morocco also plans to set a central depository body for the Casablanca stock exchange in the fourth quarter of 1997 as part of the bourse reforms launched in 1993.

"The central body is necessary for the transparency and safety of the Casablanca bourse...It will avoid disputes over commissions, facilitate transactions and help attract private enterprises," Ait Ali said.
He noted that only one private entreprise, Credor credit firm was introduced in the bourse since 1993.
($1= 9.0 dirhams)
